summary: At seven people per square mile, Plumas County is one of the least densely populated places in California — spread across 2,611 square miles of Sierra Nevada terrain that includes the northern reaches of the Sierra crest, deep river canyons carved by the Feather River's forks, and vast stretches of Plumas National Forest, which blankets a huge share of the county. The geography is genuinely dramatic: volcanic plateaus give way to alpine meadows and mixed-conifer forests, and the evening light over western ridgelines can be staggering. But that beauty comes packaged with real isolation — the local economy leans heavily on public-sector employment (federal land management, county government) and seasonal recreation, meaning switching employers without a long mountain commute or remote-work arrangement is difficult. A median home price of $327,400 against a median household income of roughly $65,000 yields a price-to-income ratio around 5:1, which is moderate by California standards but notable given limited local job options. Winters are genuinely cold — average nighttime lows sit at 36°F annually, and mountain passes can close with snow — while summers deliver nearly nine hours of daily sunshine and dry warmth that makes the trail access extraordinary. This is a place where the landscape is the main infrastructure, and whether that trade sustains you or strands you depends entirely on what you need a town to do for you.
